Resettlement · Zambia · RAPs and cut-off dates

A dated record of what stood in your project footprint on the cut-off date

Zambia’s National Resettlement Policy (2015) lists encroachment among the causes of involuntary displacement, and IFC Performance Standard 5 says a project need not compensate people who move into the project area after a cut-off date that has been clearly set and made public. AfriScan records the structures in your footprint on that date and shows what has appeared since, to support your census and asset inventory. It does not replace them. A person reviews every result.

Used in: Mining · Power & utilities · Oil & gas · Rail & roads · Project finance & ESIA

What the rules ask for

Zambian law, the resettlement plan and the lenders’ standards

Compensation under Zambian law

We found no stand-alone resettlement statute in Zambia. Compensation runs through the Lands Acquisition Act (Cap. 189), under which the President may acquire land compulsorily (s.3) with compensation (s.10) and a Compensation Advisory Board, and which excludes compensation for “undeveloped land or unutilised land” except for unexhausted improvements (s.15). The sector laws add their own rules: compensation for wayleave damage under the Electricity Act (s.23(6)), “fair and reasonable compensation” for disturbance and for damage to crops, trees and buildings under the Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024 (s.40), and “adequate compensation” under the Zambia Tanzania Pipeline Act (s.8).

A recent environmental and social assessment for a Zambian interconnector describes the process: “As required by Zambian regulations, the ESMP and RAP are submitted as standalone reports”, and the Ministry of Lands advises on the RAP at ZEMA’s request and reviews and approves the compensation measures and costs.

The cut-off date under PS5

IFC Performance Standard 5, paragraph 23: “The client is not required to compensate or assist those who encroach on the project area after the cut-off date for eligibility, provided the cut-off date has been clearly established and made public.”

The condition matters as much as the rule. A cut-off date protects a project only when it has been clearly set and made public, and when there is a record of what stood in the footprint on that date. Lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5 or the World Bank’s ESS5; the register serves either.

Zambia’s National Resettlement Policy (2015) lists “Encroachment of populations on land meant for other activities” among the causes of involuntary displacement. A dated register records the footprint as it was, so later questions are about facts, not memories.

How it works

Before the census, on the cut-off date, and after

  1. Before the census

    The imagery history of the footprint, a first count of the structures and, where the route is still open, a comparison of alignment options by the structures each would affect. Estimated households from structure counts, with the assumptions stated, help size the census teams.

  2. On the cut-off date

    A register of the structures in the footprint on the date you set, from a drone survey on that date or a satellite scene with a known capture date close to it, with an ID, coordinates and a reviewer category for each structure and the imagery date on every record.

  3. After it

    New and removed structures between the cut-off date and each later survey, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views. For a single plot or claim, a sheet of every dated image covering it.

The environmental and social study for a recent Zambian interconnector counted the houses in one section’s wayleave, noted that a few more may have been built since the cut-off date, and identified structures in an additional wayleave “based on satellite imagery interpretation”. That is the work a reviewed, dated register makes repeatable: the same method, the same IDs and the same bands at every survey.

The imagery

Why the date on the imagery matters

A cut-off record is only as good as the date of the imagery behind it. We use dated sources only: drone surveys on the day, satellite scenes with a known capture date, or imagery your team already holds with its date. Map-service basemaps, whose dates are not known, are never used as a cut-off record.

Cloud in the rainy season can delay a new capture, and archive coverage varies by place, so we tell you which dated scenes exist for your footprint before you commit, and how close to the cut-off date they are. Where the archive is too old, a new capture can be requested; its date depends on satellite availability and weather.

Drone surveys on the cut-off date are subject to the ZCAA approvals and Zambia Air Force clearance each operation requires, including a special authorisation and a ZCAA inspector on site, so they are planned into the resettlement timeline from the start. See drone law in Zambia.

Data protection

Structures in the register, names in your systems

Personal data under the Data Protection Act 2021 include location data and anything from which a person can be directly or indirectly identified (s.2), so imagery of homes linked to names, census lists or grievance files is personal data. A data controller must register with the Data Protection Commission (s.19) and “shall process and store personal data on a server or data centre located in the Republic” (s.70(1)), and sensitive personal data always stay in Zambia (s.70(3)).

Our registers carry structure IDs and coordinates, not names, so the links to households stay in your census database. Each proposal sets out the controller and processor roles and where project data will be stored. More in our notes for procurement and compliance teams.

Limits

What a cut-off baseline is not

  • A dated record of structures, with the imagery date on every record
  • Reviewer categories describing what the imagery shows
  • Change since the cut-off date, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Location checks for single plots and claims
  • A census, an asset inventory or an eligibility decision
  • Proof of use, occupancy, ownership or value
  • A count of people, or a record of who lives where
  • A land survey or a valuation

The register supports legal, compensation and community processes. Decisions on eligibility and compensation stay with the project, the authorities and the people affected.

Frequently asked questions

Does Zambian law set the cut-off date?

We found no stand-alone resettlement statute in Zambia. Compensation runs through the Lands Acquisition Act and the sector laws, such as the Electricity Act (s.23(6)), the Minerals Regulation Commission Act (s.40) and the Zambia Tanzania Pipeline Act (s.8), and the resettlement action plan sets out eligibility. Where lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5, the cut-off date must be “clearly established and made public” (para. 23). Our register records what stood in the footprint on a date you choose; it supports the cut-off-date record rather than defining it.

Is the register a substitute for the census or the asset inventory?

No. The census, the inventory of assets and improvements, the consultations and the eligibility decisions stay with your resettlement team. The register tells the field teams where the structures are, how many to expect and which ones have appeared since the cut-off date.

Our cut-off date has already passed. Can you still help?

Often, yes. We look for dated archive scenes as close to the cut-off date as the archive allows, and tell you what exists before you commit. From that record we can check claims of omission, show when a structure first appears in the dated imagery, and map what has been built in the footprint since. How much archive exists varies by place and date.

Will the register contain names or household details?

No. Our registers describe structures, with IDs and coordinates, and carry no names. Once your team links a structure to a household, the combined record is personal data under the Data Protection Act 2021, which requires registration with the Data Protection Commission and storage in Zambia unless an exception applies, so those links are kept in your own systems.

Can you tell us which structures are occupied?

No. Reviewer categories, such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction, describe what the imagery shows. They do not establish use, occupancy, ownership or value, and compensation needs ground verification.

Setting, or checking, a cut-off date?

Tell us the footprint, the census window and the date the record must reflect. We reply with the dated imagery that exists for it and a written proposal.
